title: Engagement

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shidduch, and your line was a match: an introduction made with care, the yes left to the two. Did you connect anyone? Today the match turns into a plan. Day one thousand three hundred four.

A plain china plate, wrapped in a cloth napkin. Two women, the mothers of the bride and the groom, each take an edge. A few minutes earlier, a short document was read aloud and signed in this room. Now, at a signal, the two of them bring the plate down hard on the back of a chair. It shatters inside the napkin. People clap and call out mazel tov. At some Ashkenazi weddings, this happens shortly before the ceremony. The document is today's word, and the broken plate is its exclamation mark.
screen: `A PLATE IN A NAPKIN.` → `TWO MOTHERS, ONE SIGNAL.` → `IT SHATTERS. MAZEL TOV.`

segments.voice: Tena'im. Conditions. Turn it four ways. First, what it is. The tena'im is an engagement agreement. It sets down, in writing, what the two sides have agreed: that there will be a wedding, and what each family will bring to it. In earlier generations it could be signed long before the wedding. Today, couples who keep the custom often sign it on the wedding day itself, in a side room before the ceremony. Second, why agree at all. The prophet Amos asks a question that sounds like it was written for an engagement: "Can two walk together, except they be agreed?" A marriage is two people walking a long road side by side. The tena'im says, before the walking starts: here is what we have agreed, out loud, in front of others. Third, the plate. Explanations differ, and families keep the custom without settling them. Some say it's a warning: a broken engagement, like a broken plate, can't be glued back, so treat this promise seriously. Others hear in it the same note as the glass broken under the canopy, a memory that sits inside joy, which we'll come to in a few days. Fourth, conditions today. Some couples now write tena'im in their own words, about how they hope to share a home, make decisions, disagree, and keep learning. The old idea stays the same. Conditions aren't a sign of distrust. They're how two people say plainly what they are building, before they build it.
screen: `AN AGREEMENT, IN WRITING.` · `CAN TWO WALK TOGETHER?` · `A PLATE THAT CAN'T BE GLUED.` · `TERMS IN THEIR OWN WORDS.` · then, large: `CONDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one plan together. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you share part of your life with: a partner, a roommate, a sibling, a coworker, a close friend. Choose one thing the two of you are building, even something small, like a trip, a weekly dinner, a shared project. Notice what each of you has assumed about it but never said. Pick one condition you'd like to agree on out loud: who does what, or when, or how you'll decide. Keep shaping it until it fits in one kind sentence. The bell holds the time.
Tena'im: conditions. The engagement agreement, read and signed, and at some weddings sealed with a broken plate. Today's word.
Your line: conditions. Today, make one plan with someone, and say the terms out loud, kindly, so you both agree. Day one thousand three hundred four.
